title: The Pay Cut and the Missing Stock
text:
In the late 1980s a manufacturing company lost two large contracts and decided to cut pay by 15 percent for ten weeks at two of its three plants, rather than lay anyone off. The organizational psychologist Jerald Greenberg was able to study what happened next.

At one plant, the company president held a long meeting with the workers. He explained at length why the cut was necessary and that it would be temporary, expressed regret and answered their questions. At the second plant, a vice president announced the cut in a short meeting of about fifteen minutes, with little explanation and no expression of sympathy. The third plant had no pay cut and served as a comparison.

Greenberg tracked employee theft through the company's standard records of missing inventory. At the plant without a cut, theft stayed at its usual low level. At both pay cut plants it rose, but it rose far more at the plant where the cut had been announced curtly. More workers also quit there. When normal pay was restored, theft returned to its usual level.
lesson: Bad news delivered with honesty and respect causes far less damage than the same news delivered coldly. How you explain a decision is part of the decision.
location: Three plants of a US manufacturing company
source: Greenberg, J. (1990). Employee theft as a reaction to underpayment inequity: The hidden cost of pay cuts. Journal of Applied Psychology, 75(5), 561-568.
